The house resumed from Wednesday, March 9, consideration of the motion of the Prime Minister that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March'' in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.

Yesterday, at the close of an impassioned speech in which moderation was conspicuous by its absence, the hon. the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) exhibited a rather delightful piece of humour when he asked the cooperation of my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), myself and others on this side of the house. Cooperation in what? Cooperation with whom? We are ready to cooperate, but can we do so by supporting the measure which is now before the chair? It is a direct refusal of cooperation; it is a challenge to parliamentary institutions. Does not the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) realize that he is going altogether too far in the direction of personal power and autocracy? He is asking the elected representatives of the people of Canada to abdicate the control and sovereignty of parliament. He is asking full authority to legislate by order in council, to amend statutes, to decide anything while parliament is in session, to enter into any expenditure of public money without previous parliamentary authorization; and he kindly suggests and generously offers to communicate to us the decision after it will have been reached. Sir, is not that an utter disrespect for and contempt of parliament? Is it not adding insult to injury? How can we cooperate upon such a basis?
We have been elected to a legislative body, and the seriousness of the situation and the complexity of the problems which face this country at the present time make it all the more necessary that we should all endeavour to find the solution of these problems. We are willing to work; we are willing to sit on committees; we are willing to consider any proposal, any measure which this government has to offer; we are willing to adopt such measures if they are in the public interest. But we are not ready to vest in the Prime Minister a dictatorship, to transfer to him and his cabinet the rights and authorities of this parliament, and to delegate to him the

mandate which we have received from our constituencies. How can we cooperate when the decision has been reached before being submitted to parliament? How can we cooperate when the policies of the country are devised, decided and executed by order in council, and more particularly when important matters are decided one way and modified, altered, changed or cancelled before we have even had the chance of knowing it? How can we cooperate when this government one day preaches the expenditure of public money for the relief of distress in the country, and the next day preaches strict economy, curtails expenditures, retires civil servants, cuts salaries and so forth. Our rulers, like Penelope, the wife of the great Ulysses, are undoing during the night the work that they have done during the preceding day.
You must admit, Mr. Speaker, that it is rather difficult for reasonable men to cooperate with inconsistency, whim and whimsicality. No executive in the world has achieved the autocratic power of the present Canadian cabinet-I am speaking of countries with representative parliaments. I think the nearest parallel in history is to be found in the Committee of Public Safety during the terror of the French revolution. Like this government, that committee had an all powerful executive, controlling all things; like this government, that committee had the support of a majority in the convention. All the powers were held by that committee and it became such a despotism that it was the strongest and most ruthless which history has ever recorded. Of course, I do not suggest that this will happen in Canada; I do not believe the Prime Minister will go beyond certain limits. But has a free parliament the right to establish such a dictatorship? Has it the right to take a chance? Are we justified in abdicating all control and placing the rights and liberties of the Canadian people in the hands of one man, however distinguished he may be? The right hon. gentleman possesses great qualities but he will pardon me if I say that he possesses also some substantial imperfections. He has some characteristic features which are not unmixed qualities, and history proves that no man is great enough to endure well-nigh absolute power without a certain amount of moral weakening and that uncontrolled despotism always inflicts serious injury to the body politic.
May I quote the words of my right hon. friend uttered while he was in opposition. At that time he was complaining that the then Minister of Labour, Mr. Heenan, was endeavouring to enact legisluation which gave 
the power to make regulations in order to carry out the provisions of the act, and here is what he said:
I consider the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) a fair-minded minister but I do not think that it is in the interests of Canada that powers so great should be conferred upon any one individual under the modern democratic form of government where the temptations for abuse are as great as the powers here conferred.
The first departure by this government from sound constitutional practices occurred at the special session of 1930. At that time my right hon. friend asked this house to vote the sum of twenty million dollars to be used for such purposes and under such terms and conditions as the governor general in council would prescribe. That was a violation of the well known principle that the commons has full and unrestricted control over the destination of public money. Every sum taken from the consolidated revenue fund must be applied to a special purpose; it must be voted by parliament either under a statute, when the expense is a permanent one, or by an annual vote in the estimates, as is generally the case. That is the only possible way for parliament to retain its control over the expenditure of public money. In either case the destination must be described and at no time until this government took office had this principle been denied or violated. As my right hon. leader said, even during the war Sir Robert Borden not only specified the amount of money which he asked parliament to vote for the carrying on of the war but he gave the details as to the destination of that money. He said that so much was needed for expenditures connected with the Niobe or the Rainbow, so much for the purchase of a submarine or so much for the purchase of horses. Parliament always was given the fullest details. Had my right hon. friend then been on this side of the house and the government of the day had attempted to do that which is being attempted to-day we would have heard that which Dicey, Anson and Redlich say in the most eloquent terms.

My right hon. friend threatened us with the calamity of his being unable to attend the Imperial conference, and as we could not afford to suffer his absence we allowed this measure to go through. Last year it became still worse. Chapter 58 of the statutes of 1931 was passed, and it is now proposed to resurrect this measure and extend its provisions for two months. I then stated that the bill gave a blank cheque to the government and the power to expend any amount of money for any purpose whatever. I stated, and my words can be found in Hansard, that the provisions of the act which permitted the taking of any steps to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada gave to the government the powers given to the parliament of Canada under section 91 of the British North America Act. I protested against that legislation but we were told that our misgivings were unfounded, that the things we feared would never happen. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) discarded all our statements and said that the words "peace, order and good government" were inserted in the statute to give authority to parliament to vote a blank cheque for the purpose of relieving distress and unemployment. My hon. friend said:
If the bill is not founded upon the theory that it is necessary to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada, then parliament would have no authority to pass it. Without these words the bill in the form in which it is enacted into law might be set aside when challenged in the courts.
And again:
We recognize this emergency by the adoption of these words from the British North America Act, and they were placed in the bill as the foundation of our authority to pass such an enactment. They have nothing to do with the question of enforcement; they are merely a declaration to give us the jurisdiction which we know we have under the circumstances but of which vve want to be sure. . . . We are guaranteeing relief in order to maintain peace, order and good government. That makes it constitutionally certain that the bill will not be set aside.
The Prime Minister, when he referred to that provision about law and order, spoke only of possible troubles in Canada and said that it was good policy, good statesmanship on the part of the government to provide for any such disturbances. He said:
It is not for a moment to be thought that an insignificant number of strongly vocal persons shall be able so to affect the populace of this country as to make it impossible for us, in cooperation together as Canadians, to work out our destiny. I say that class, happily, is few- in number. But in this present situation they now see an opportunity propitious to the prosecution of their pernicious political doctrines. This is a land of freedom.
And so on. He continues:
If the government is given reason to believe, as there may be some cause for its so believing, that there is a settled purpose in the minds of a considerable number of people-not large, numerically, but scattered over the various parts of Canada-to take action against the maintenance of law and order, or make attempts to impede the difficult task with which we are charged, then we will take such action as in the judgment of the executive of this country, the cabinet who are the board of directors for the time being administering the affairs of this country, as will free this country from those wrho have proved themselves unworthy of our Canadian citizenship.
At no place in their argument did either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Justice suggest or represent or intimate that this law would be made use of to amend the statutes of the country generally. What has occurred? The Prime Minister, in the course of his remarks when introducing this resolution. spoke about an order in council concerning the returns to be made by the insurance companies. When I asked him whether there were other orders in council under that clause relating to peace, order and good government, he said that he did not know of any, but the Minister of Justice whispered to him that there was one concerning the prohibition of the export of gold.
Yesterday some orders in council were laid on the table of the house and I have been able to find at least three of four or more of them passed under this provision of peace,

The first I find is order in council P.C. 2238, guaranteeing repayment to the chartered banks mentioned in it, of the amounts of money advanced by them to the Canadian Cooperative Wheat Producers, Limited, in connection with the crop of the year 1930. I do not think my right hon. friend has treated parliament properly in that regard. And so forth. I have no time to read it all, but I draw the attention of the house to the fact that the promise, the undertaking, had been given prior to the session of parliament-it is so stated in the order in council -that there would be legislation to implement the guarantee of the government. No legislation was introduced in parliament al-

though the matter was referred to on three different occasions. Then, after the session was over, an order in council is passed as a substitute for the legislation that should have been passed by parliament. There were no communistic activities in connection with this.
Then there are three orders in council, again guaranteeing advances by the banks to the marketing agencies mentioned in those orders. I have not time to refer to them.
The second order in council to which I wish to refer is the one dealing with the prohibition of the export of gold. This was passed on Monday, the nineteenth day of October, 1931. But before I refer to it, I would ask the government at least to submit to parliament legislation to ratify the order in council with regard to the guarantee of the advances by the banks.

As regards the order in council dealing with the prohibition of the export of gold, that again is passed under the provision regarding peace, order and good government. A penalty is fixed of a fine of SI ,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years, or both fine and imprisonment. It is stated in the order that these provisions shall come into force on the 19th day of October, 1931, and shall continue in full force and effect until the first day of March, 1932. If this order is renewed or extended, I hope it will be done by an act of parliament and not by a juggling of the calendar by substituting May for March as is proposed to be done by the resolution now before the house.
Then on the 27th October, 1931, order in council P.C. 2693 was passed, virtually amending the Bank Act, authorizing the banks to make to the government returns with regard to securities in another way than that fixed by the Bank Act. It also has force and effect until the first March, 1932. I ask the government, if this order in council is to be extended, that this should be done by act of parliament. The Bank Act is one of the most important acts. It is sacred legislation. It is different from the others in this, that we have a revision of the Bank Act every ten years, when a committee of this house studies any proposed changes most carefully. Surely the Bank Act should not be amended by order in council without authority of parliament.

Then on December 16, 1931, P.C. 3087 was passed on the recommendation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), increasing the strength of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police by three hundred men, with an added expenditure of $274,135. I do not want to comment upon that, but perhaps it is the reason for the fine parades we are witnessing on different occasions around the parliament buildings.
Then there was the order in council virtually amending the Insurance Act. Section 34 of the Insurance Act provides that the stocks held by the insurance companies must be valued at their market value. That was amended by order in council. It is stated in that order in council that the privy council has virtually declared that the Insurance Act is ultra vires and that it is proposed at the next session of parliament to bring in a new law which the law officers of the crown believe will be intra vires. But before this new law is put into force we have this order in council. I have seen the bill which is presently before the Senate and I notice that section 54 of that bill is exactly the same as section 34 of the Insurance Act as it was. There is no change made there at all. Will that order in council be extended for another year? If so, I say again that this parliament has the right to discuss and pass upon such a matter. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is there one of those five or six orders in council which I have mentioned passed in the interests of the unemployed? This whole legislation was passed presumably for the relief of distress and unemployment and the clause about peace, order and good government was included only to give authority to the government for that purpose. But these orders in council which were passed concerning the insurance business and banking and the mounted police, were they orders in council passed in the interests of the unemployed? They took the place of acts of parliament, which is exactly what we am-621
foresaw would happen as the use to which the clause would be put when the legislation was before the house.
But bad as that legislation was, the present proposal is many times worse. This parliament is in session and the government is asking power to amend to-morrow a statute which we may pass to-day in this House of Commons. The suggestion that the rights of parliament will.be safeguarded merely by tabling at the next session of parliament any orders in council that may be passed is preposterous. It reduces parliament to a formless debating society, carrying on in a vacuum of futility.
Sir, the legislative function is to formulate what is to be and what should be the law of the country. The function of the executive is to carry out the law as formulated by this parliament. It is parliament that has the power to decide what the law is and what the law should be. It is parliament that has the control of the treasury, of the levying of taxes and of the manner of spending those taxes. It is the only effective agency in any British House of Commons for controlling the departments of government. The goal of democratic government is a satisfactory understanding between those two branches of government. Fundamental laws have defined what are the proper functions of each. The struggle of the House of Commons in England extending over many hundreds of years was carried on to ensure the control of parliament over the executive-not the control of the executive over parliament.
The Prime Minister pleaded that to proceed in this way would give greater convenience to the government in the serious conditions that now face the country. Doubtless absolute and autocratic power is more convenient than a free government. But does Canada want that? Our system is one of check and balance to make it sure that none of the divisions of the government shall become so powerful as to have the others at its mercy.
When in opposition my right hon. friend the Prime Minister referred frequently to that clever book of the present Lord Chief Justice of Great Britain, Lord Hewart, entitled The New Despotism. I might say that the Prime Minister's is a newer and stricter and narrower despotism. I have here a fine quotation of Lord Hewart which I should like to put on Hansard if I had time, but perhaps at some other stage of the bill I shall have the pleasure of doing so. But Lord Hewart was speaking only of regulations which permitted the departments virtually to make the laws of the land. He never even dreamt that

With the increase in debt amounting to $2,000,000,000, it will be seen that $666,000,000 was well spent, $666,000,000 was wasted and $666,000,000 was stolen by the profiteers.
What proportion of that $2,000,000,000 was spent on railways?

I shall not try to educate my hon. friend. He is generally mixed up with the figures he gives to the house so I am not surprised that he does not understand mine. The latter part of the money was spent for McAdam shovels, old horses, Valoartier butter, drugs-I will not mention names-and bully beef.
And bacon.

Mr. Speaker, I am compelled to take part in this debate because of the remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Manion), who asked for some constructive proposal from this house to assist in dealing with the question of unemployment in Canada. Before proceeding to offer any constructive proposals, I should like to make it clear that I do not agree with the statement of policy of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in regard to the responsibility of this parliament so far as unemployment is concerned. The Prime Minister said that the duty of caring for the unemployed rested primarily upon the municipalities; if the municipality was unable to deal with the situation, it should appeal to the province for assistance, and if the province was unable to deal with the problem it should apply to the Dominion government. I would point out that this parliament has control of the vital economic policies which determine whether or not the people of Canada are going to have employment. We have control of immigration; we have control of tariffs; we have control of banking, currency and credit. Whether or not the people are to have employment depends upon the policies laid down under these three heads. The municipalities and the provinces are helpless in the matter; they cannot protect themselves against unemployment if certain policies are carried out by this parliament. The government has said that this is a national emergency, and I am sure that the municipalities and provinces are not responsible.
Let us deal first with immigration. I would refer hon. members to the statement made about a week ago by the Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Gordon). He pointed out that in the sixteen months ended July 31, 1930, about 221,000 people were brought into Canada, of whom 99,367
were adult males. He then went on to say that many of these people are to be found to-day among the unemployed in our large cities. These people have contributed largely to the unemployment problem which is facing the country to-day. Why should this government say that the responsibility of taking care of the unemployed rests primarily upon the municipalities? It does not rest there at all, it rests upon, this parliament. It was the federal government that carried out the policy of immigration under which these people, who are now unemployed came to Canada and who, under our policy, are a charge upon the municipalities.
In that speech the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) referred to the unemployment relief measure which was brought down by the government in 1930 and under which the house voted $20,000,000, the bulk of it to be used for unemployment relief work. The minister says, as reported1 on page 441 of Hansard of this year, that the measure resulted in a total expenditure of $70,472.832, the federal	government's share
being $17,372,848. In my opinion this policy was absolutely unfair to the provinces and to the municipalities.	Of the $70,000,000
which was spent, only $17,000,000 was supplied by the federal government, a government that came into office as the result of a campaign in which they promised, if returned to power, to cure unemployment. AH they did in that year was to pay one-fourth of the amount that was spent on unemployment relief. On behalf of the municipalities and the provinces I want to protest against the policy which has been carried out in that respect. Of course the provinces and the municipalities were helpless in the matter; they had to accept the policy of the federal government.
As regards tariffs, both major parties in the house agree that the tariff policy of this country affects employment. That being so, why do we not frankly admit that unemployment is a federal matter? The unemployment which exists in Canada is primarily due to policies which are enforced by the federal government. The best minds in the world to-day admit that the money policies which have been in force in various countries during the last few years are primarily the cause of unemployment, and certainly the municipalities and the provinces have no way of protecting themselves against money policies which may be adopted by this parliament.
I want to point out further that the Prime Minister, when he was touring Canada during the election campaign of 1930, did not promise

that if he became Prime Minister he would assist the provinces and municipalities in caring for the unemployment which they were unable to take care of themselves; he said that he would cure unemployment. But when he comes into office, the first year he is in power he assumes a liability for only one-quarter of the total amount which is spent in that regard. Last year when the municipalities and provinces became so hard up, he had to assume a larger share.
The Dominion government could create employment in this country. They have an act giving them the very widest powers imaginable. If they have not cured unemployment, the inference is plain that they either will not or cannot suggest the policies that will cure it. I should like to point out that the policy which has been in force for dealing with unemployment relief, that is, direct relief, has not been fair. As I understand the matter, the municipalities must pay at least one-third of the amount which is expended upon direct relief. In order to protect itself from a large influx of the unemployed, one city must be careful not to give any more relief than that given by another. The result has been that at least in some cities, an unemployed man cannot get any relief unless he has been a resident there for three months. Cases have come to my attention where men who came to Calgary from other municipalities could not secure any relief except by begging from door to door. That is not the proper policy for dealing with unemployment or for affording direct relief. The federal government, should, I think, have assumed the major share of the expenditure for the direct relief which was given.
In regard to the unemployment relief work which was undertaken, there was far too much delay in securing approval of the different works, because they had to be passed upon by three different authorities. The federal government would have been well advised to send one man or, if necessary, two or three of them, to western Canada with ample power to agree on the spot as to what work was to be done, thus permitting the federal, provincial and municipal authorities to agree upon a particular work and put it into operation immediately, instead of having various suggestions passing back and forth among these different authorities. Much of the work that was undertaken was held up until very late in the fall; in fact, some of it was undertaken after winter had set in, and I do not think we got as good value for the money 
expended as we should have secured had the work been arranged directly and expeditiously.
I should like to suggest that the unemployed people in Canada be registered. We should know' what kind of work they are fitted for, and each man who records himself as in need of employment or assistance should be given some kind of registration card or certificate. Two or three full meals a day should be provided for every unemployed man until work is offered to him. I would suggest, I suppose I had better say a non-partisan commission, representing all industries in Canada, including agriculture, to study the country's needs and the possibilities of creating employment, and to see that employment is provided in the way of constructive work so that we may get value for the money expended.
I want to make a definite, and, I think, a constructive proposal to the government. The particular work which I believe might be undertaken, without waiting for a great deal of survey, would be the construction of homes in Canada, decent homes for our people to live in. If we wish to get people interested in this country, people to have faith in Canada, as the advertisements say, there is no better way of doing so than by getting them into homes of their own. There must be at least 2,000.000 families in Canada, and I think it is safe to assume that one-tenth of them have no decent homes in which to live. That gives us a field for a great deal of employment. I am not going to suggest that the government should start to build this year 200,000 houses, but we might very well make a start with at least 50.000. I do not think there is anything impossible about that. I believe the construction of 50,000 homes at this time would afford employment to the bulk of the men who are now unemployed. Those houses can be built out of Canadian lumber, Canadian cement; in fact, I think we have in this country industries which will supply all the materials for those houses, for example, saw mills, cement mills, brickyards, and most of them idle.
Where is there a shortage of houses in this country?

I shall point that out in
just a minute. We have, as I say, all these building materials available, and we certainly have plenty of workmen wanting jobs. Why not bring the rvorkmen and the materials together and build the homes where they are needed? They are needed both in the country districts and in the cities. In the country districts there are odd cases where families

are still living in dugouts; on the prairies there are thousands of families living in shacks, and those people would be glad to have real houses to live in. I can show my hon. friend who has questioned me, families who are living in shacks built of one-ply of boards and one-ply of building paper, and who this winter have endured once or twice a temperature of twenty-five degrees below zero. The coal they are burning has been furnished in some cases by the municipality. There is no doubt about a great number of houses being required in certain cities in Canada. I find in the Halifax Citizen a report which says that a housing commission in Halifax has just made an investigation and a report which reveals conditions in Halifax that rival the slums of China. Perhaps that will convince my hon. friend that some new houses are needed. I shall quote very briefly from that report itself:
The problem of housing in Halifax has of late challenged the attention, of the lovers of our city and of those interested in the health and welfare of our people, and well it may, for Halifax is infested with a high percentage, per house population, of tumbledown shacks where whole families eat, sleep, bathe and live in a single room, where cellars reek with filth and vermin, where sewerage runs riot-hovels unfit for human habitation and typical of the worst slum conditions to be heard of anywhere.
The report continues:
There are many cases of excessive rentals and some flagrant instances of overcrowding and overcharging. A few illustrations may be given from the survey files:
One room in cellar occupied by five persons, per month, ten dollars.
One room in cellar occupied by seven persons, per month, six dollars.
Mr. Speaker, I would appeal to the members for order while I read these few figures. I would like to read the last two again so that some hon. gentlemen may become aware of the housing conditions existing in the city of Halifax, as reported by this housing commission:
One room in cellar occupied by five persons, per month, ten dollars.
One room in cellar occupied by seven persons, per month, six dollars.
Living quarters in loft of barn, six persons, per month, twelve dollars.
Four rooms occupied by nine persons, per month, twenty-five dollars.
Seven rooms occupied by twenty-eight persons, per month, one hundred and fifty dollars.
Two cellar rooms occupied by eight persons, per month, ten dollars.
One dark room, door only, occupied by three persons, per month, ten dollars.
The report goes on to say:
It is conditions such as these which may yet bring to Nova Scotia a maximum rent as well as a minimum wage.
I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that I believe that those conditions can be duplicated in some other cities in Canada. I remember quite well that a few years ago a witness from the city of Montreal appeared before the committee on agriculture and colonization when we were inquiring into the question of immigration, and told us of conditions in the city of Montreal which were practically on the same lines as set forth in this report of the Halifax housing commission.
Have I said enough to convince hon. members of this house that there are houses needed in Canada for our population? How can we expect to raise in Canada a decent, God-fearing, healthy population such as we should have if they are to be housed under conditions such as obtain in that old and fair city of Halifax, conditions which I am sure are duplicated in many other Canadian cities? In what better way could the government provide employment than by building houses for our people? That is certainly one thing that is needed. We do not need more food in Canada, though we do need some way of getting the food from the farms to the people in the cities who are hungry. I believe that there is plenty of clothing and plenty of shoes in Canada, but there are not enough houses to accommodate our population. The government from now on I think need not say that there has not been a constructive proposal put before them in connection with unemployment.
I had expected that before this some hon. member would have asked me: Where will you get the money? I am quite surprised that that question has not been asked. In reply I think I had better quote the words which are attributed to the Prime Minister, who, speaking at Montreal in the last campaign in reply to a lady in the audience who asked where he was going to get all the money required to fulfil his promises, said, "From taxation, where we always get it." That would have been my answer if somebody had asked me that question. But if I had my way, that is not where I would get it, because we are already taxing industry out of existence, and I do not think we should add to its burdens to get money even to build houses. I am going to suggest a way of getting the money which I think is orthodox or very nearly so. It has at least an air of respectability.
I would create a corporation and officer it with a few public spirited citizens, practical men who I believe could be secured and who would give their services for a few thousand dollars per year. I would charge them with

this work. When they begin to build the houses they could issue bonds, which would be secured by a mortgage on these houses. Those bonds could be taken to our treasury board just as the banks bring bonds to the treasury board, and the treasury board could advance dominion notes against the bonds in the same way as dominion notes are advanced to the banks. This building corporation could then pay for materials and the wages of its workmen with these dominion notes. The houses would be sold on easy terms, extending perhaps over ten or fifteen years, with a rate of interest not exceeding, I would hope, about two per cent; and as the payments came in, the money could be used to retire the dominon notes issued to construct the houses. I think, Mr. Speaker, that this is a reasonable proposal. I am not going to be too specific in suggesting detailed plans for carrying out the proposal. I should only get into difficulty if I did so. I am quite willing to leave the details to the government to be worked out, but I am quite sure that if they picked out the right men, and they are available in Canada, there would be nothing impossible in working out such a scheme. If necessarj' the cooperation of the municipalities could be invited. Montreal, Toronto, Halifax, and many other cities in Canada would, I think, be glad to cooperate with the Dominion government in working out such a plan. The municipalities themselves have not got the money to spend. Some of them I know are practically bankrupt to-day, and they are only spending what the bankers will allow them to spend, but they might assume some responsibility in connection with this housing scheme.
I could go on and suggest one or two other proposals to the government. I should be glad to do it, as I am sure many other hon. members of this house would be, if the government really wants constructive proposals, I am sure that we can find plenty of employment for every man and woman in this country. If the farms in western Canada could this summer employ ad the men they really need, they would take fifty thousand men, probably more, off the labour market. Several thousand men could be put to work ridding the road allowances and vacant lands in western Canada of weeds. That would be very constructive work; it would add to the national wealth, and I believe we are justified in spending money that will result in increasing the national wealth. The money which would be put into circulation by a housing scheme such as I have suggested would increase trade, and as the dominion taxes are largely levied on 
trade, it would increase the revenues of the country. Moreover, it would assist the government in balancing its budget and would relieve it of a large expenditure for direct unemployment relief. I would suggest also-and I suppose there is not much likelihood of my suggestion being accepted-that if any such proposal be undertaken a certain percentage of the wages of the workmen engaged be reserved and set to their credit in what might be termed an unemployment insurance fund to take care of them next winter when they are out of work. I would suggest that in future we should not endeavour to do road work or work of that nature in the dead of winter. It is largely a waste of effort and money. Let us put those men to work in the spring and summer months, and save from their wages enough money to take care of them in the winter time.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. member who has just spoken will pardon me if I do not follow his very interesting argument. At this juncture I just wish to consider the constitutional issue arising out of the proposal of the government.
Ever since gentlemen opposite came into power I have endeavoured to reduce to a minimum my criticisms of their executive policies, especially in regard to unemployment. But when the measure for which an extension is now proposed was brought forward last year I made the observation, and I repeat it to-night, that in times of great crises, in times of war, famine or economic depression, there are two dangers to avoid. One danger is to stick too narrowly to the strict letter of the law and thereby impede the action of the powers that be, whether they be federal, provincial or municipal governments, because, after all, the salvation of the people is the supreme law. The other danger is, that, confronted with an emergency, with new problems cropping up suddenly or taking abnormal proportions, parliaments and peoples are tempted by a clean sweep to do away with the most precious safeguards that experience and the wisdom of centuries had brought them to adopt for their own safety. When during the emergency session 'the government asked for S20,000,000, I entered a mild protest; but at that time I did not push my views very far because, after all, the amount-of money was limited and it was simply and solely to be applied-or perhaps misapplied, which expression might (be used concerning every amount of money we vote-for a specific object.

Last year, however, I .protested strongly against the unlimited powers asked by the government,-powers which, in effect, would permit the ministry to make, amend, or repeal laws during the recess. The Prime Minister gave some reasons for asking passage of the bill; and those reasons he reiterated this year. Of course, admittedly, it is much simpler for a government not to be handicapped by the shackles of parliamentary institutions; no doubt about that. An economist with very broad views, Mr. Einzig, points out that, thanks to the absolute power put into his hands, Signor Mussolini was capable of dealing effectively with certain problems in Italy which probably could not have been solved by a regularly constituted government. No doubt about that; no doubt at all. Likewise, at the other end of the European situation, both geographically and constitutionally, no doubt Lenin and, now, Mr. Stalin, have been capable of accomplishing things, good or bad, which not even our Prime Minister could accomplish.
I hope hon. members will not think I am comparing either the men or their talents. I am simply comparing institutions and functions. I do not quite partake of the surprise or indignation of my Liberal friends at the attitude of the Prime Minister. It was to be expected, sir. No doubt the Conservatives knew, when they chose their leader, what kind of man they were choosing.

A very powerful man,
I admit; I have said that very often. Even before the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) was one of the obedient followers of the Prime Minister I made that statement. I have known the Prime Minister for a much longer time than has the Minister of Marine, and I have much personal admiration and friendship for him. Perhaps he would not want me to state my friendship in public, because he might be compromised with some of his friends. Intimately, however, I think, he accepts those terms of friendship. When he was chosen leader of his party I predicted that if he ever came to power we would have the most authentic autocrat Canada has ever known. He has the will, the talent and the power. To a certain extent the people of Canada have got what they deserved. I warned my friends in my little constituency that if the Conservatives came to power unemployment would not be ended. I advised those people to discard ninety-five per cent of the promises made by the Conservatives
to that effect, and told them to await results. The year has passed, and results show they were justified in waiting. But as to the kind of government the people of Canada have, they have what they voted for.
Let us come back to the measure now before us. May I say it is a logical sequel to the political temperament of the leader of the government? He was absolutely himself when the other day he said, "I cannot conceive any other means by which I can rule this country." Of course he cannot; of course not. A man is never as powerful as when he rules according to his own temperament. The weak leader is the one who rules according to the dictates of his friends, although he does not believe in them. A certain ruler in France said, "Oh well, I must follow them; I am their leader." The Prime Minister of Canada has reversed that. He has said, "You boys follow me, and obey; I am your leader,"-and he is, no doubt.
So we are faced with dictation and autocracy. I am told that this afternoon some hon. members opposite expressed their pride and contentment upon being reduced to the state which, by historical comparison, I shall endeavour directly to describe. Given those circumstances, if the government intends to play its game fully and openly I can see no reason why, after this law is passed, parliament should not be dissolved immediately. Why keep us here? We want to economize; why spend the money of the country, and ours? Why deprive the poor people of so much public money and keep us here sitting, talking, listening, drinking and eating, if the government of the country is to be reduced to the dictation of one man, with, of course, such number and quality of executioners as may be needed?
Powerful governments were carried on in that manner; great empires were built up for a time. The power of the sultans of Constantinople once threatened to cover practically the whole of the basin of the Mediterranean, north Africa, Spain, the south of France, the whole of Asia Minor, Egypt, Greece^ and all those countries that have since become what are called the Balkan nations. No doubt that great empire could not have been built up with a parliament. No doubt the manner in which the sultans made and imposed their laws made them much more effective than any law that can be passed or framed under the guidance of a parliament. There is not the slightest doubt that if George III and Lord North had persisted in their endeavours to rule their newly acquired empire in the manner which brought about the rev-

Unemployment Continuance Act
olution of the United States, and had succeeded in bringing the minds, the souls and the bodies of all the liberty loving British peoples to the state of subserviency in which hundreds of millions of people submitted to the dictates of the sultans, the British empire would have been more united than it is. I mean it would have been more united by a rule of iron, but less united by the love of liberty and the adherence to a standard of government which has never had a superior in the history of the world.
What was the government of the sultans? Of course the sultans by themselves could not do everything, and that will be the experience of the Prime Minister before very long, with all his great ability. He is now ruling his majority; there is no difficulty in that. He is ruling his cabinet, also without much difficulty; but before very long he will find out that after all a man, even a superman, has only twenty-four hours a day in which to eat, sleep and work. He will find out that even from his point of view he will be obliged to get someone to carry on some part of his work. I believe I begin to perceive in what manner he will execute his one-manmade laws; it will be in a manner similar to that of the old sultans. They had two bodies of men to aid them in ruling their empire; they maintained physical peace with the aid of the janizaries. We are beginning to have them around this house. I met one of them at one of the posterns of this parliament; he nearly took my cap off my head and asked me what business I had coming here. This was no longer ago than last week. Then the sultans carried on their inside government with a very peculiar kind of executive body, the eunuchs. They were very effective and devoted servants; not much more so than those who surround the Prime Minister, but on the whole they were very obedient. Of course once in a while the janizaries poiniarded the sultan or the eunuchs hanged him and threw his body in the Bosphorus, but the system worked for some time.
Evidently the Prime Minister is preparing this parliament to fill the functions of those civil servants of the sultans. I am given to understand that some of the young members of this house this afternoon expressed their pride at being reduced to that state; but even at my age I do object. The old sultans at least had one excuse; they kept around them harems of wives and concubines; and no doubt so far as that portion of their administrative work was concerned it was a proper thing to secure civil servants carefully prepared for the work of looking after that portion of their

government. But I do not believe that to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada, to give food to the poor or work to the unemployed, it is absolutely necessary to reduce parliament to that state. Perhaps in the senate we could do so-as a matter of fact I think the passing of time has attended to that-and intellectually at least it would seem that a number of hon. members of this house are also prepared to fulfil that role. But, sir, I claim that in the year of grace, 1932, in a country built up by the representatives of two of the most civilized European countries, with the addition in the last twentydive years of newcomers from other free, Christian countries, Canada is not yet prepared for that kind of government.
There are two considerations urged by the government in asking for these extraordinary powers. The one is the consideration of money, and the other is what I might call the legal or administrative consideration. Let us consider the question of money first. Let us suppose that last year, before realizing exactly what was the position in Canada, before being able to measure the needs of all the provinces, the municipalities and the different classes in Canada, the government conscientiously felt that they could not exactly state the amount of money they required. At least they could have asked for a certain sum, and they could do that this year. If that amount did not prove sufficient they could have done what all governments have done under regularly constituted authority; they could have issued governor general's warrants to carry on their work of helping those who required help, and later asked parliament to ratify the expenditure of the amount over and above the sum of money voted at the previous session. What reasonable man would have refused that ratification-of course, without divesting himself of I will not say the privilege but the essential duty of members of parliament, which is to look into the manner in which that money was spent? That must be apparent to anyone who has taken the trouble to read British history, whether he be English, Scotch or French by origin; to whatever race he may belong; who feels some degree of pride, call it racial pride, intellectual pride or, as in my case, political pride, in the traditions of British government.
I repeat what I said last year: The essential function of the House of Commons and the representatives of the people is to control the exchequer. For centuries and centuries the British House of Commons did not pass laws; the legislative power was vested practically in the hands of the king and the lords. Later

ordinary powers, then why do these gentlemen
on, with the evolution of time, the House of Commons, forced, so to speak, by the people whose cry increased, and who were acquiring a new sense of their rights and of their liberties, the commons asserted their duty, as the elected representatives of the masses who pay taxation, to control legislation as well as the spending of money; because after all, especially in modern times when economics play such a role in the life of a nation, you cannot separate the power of legislation from the power of taxation. They go hand in hand.
Now, with regard to this new measure, parliament is in session. The government, or rather the Prime Minister, who is the whole government, can come every day and make suggestions, or even charge one of his followers, whether a minister or not, to make suggestions. He can always come to parliament from day to day; and by looking at the order paper you can see that at least the government does preserve some show of consideration for the legislative power of the house. The ministry ask us to pass this bill and that, to amend this or the other law. Why come with a piece of blank legislation and ask us, while we are here in session to discuss every measure proposed, to abdicate our functions and give the government a free hand? They pay no more regard to us than, not to any man on the street, but to any dog or cat. They say to us virtually, "Pass such laws as we want to have passed".
It may be said that the government will not abuse its powers. Sir, many times men who have encroached upon the liberties of the people -have made use of that argument. Many times servile followers of would-be dictators have also made that appeal to the people: "Place your confidence in this or that man because you know he will not abuse it". Well, if intelligent and reasonable men have learned one thing from the history of government it is -that the danger is precisely to invest men who inspire confidence in the people with unlimited powers. Once the precedent is made, once the power is granted and put into the hands of one man, it may be misused to-morrow either by that man or by someone else unworthy of the confidence of the people. Time and again I have heard the right hon. gentleman, when sitting on this side of the house, quoting from his marvelous memory and knowledge of British history this, that and the other precedent of British parliamentary government, urging that we respect those sacred bases of parliamentary institutions. Now, sir, if precedents are good when you are in opposition, to prevent a government from abusing
ask us now to -pass legislation which all precedents condemn from top to bottom?
There is just one evidence I wish to cite with regard to the abuse 'that can be made of these powers. Reading Hansard, I notice a slight altercation which took place yesterday between my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), with reference to the order in council, or rather the law passed in the form of an order in council, amending the Finance and Bank Acts and putting into the hands of the government the arbitrary power of saying whether or not people who had entered into engagements in New York to pay their bonds or notes in gold should do so. The Minister of Railways has insinuated that that power has been exercised only for the prevention of speculation. The Minister of Railways is very patriotic. He trembled at the idea that some unworthy Canadians would take Canadian gold and ship it to New York to make twenty per cent profit out of it. Is he sure that of the five million dollars which his leader has permitted the banks to export to New York, not one dollar has been used in speculation? What guarantee has the government that the clients of the banks did not play the New York market with the gold shipped under special authorization given them by the government? But I will cite a counter instance. An acquaintance of mine in Montreal carries on a large boot and shoe industry-not one of these new mushroom concerns in which there is no responsibility, but a factory established nearly fifty years ago. This concern was managed by the father of the man to whom I refer, and has been in this man's charge ever since. He is practically the owner of it. The factory employs hundreds of men and operates, I believe, in the constituency of Maisonneuve, in the eastern section of Montreal. Last fall he had to ask himself the question whether he should carry on his operations, for he was losing money every day, every week, every month. He gathered his men together and said to them:	You worked for my father,
some of you; some of you have worked in this factory all your lives, and others from ten to twenty

 years. If I consulted only my ledgers and my personal interests I would close the gates to-morrow; or I could spare about one-fifth of you and continue employing the rest half days. But I can do something else which I am putting up to you: I -am prepared to keep all of you at salaries reduced -by ten -per cent, and in doing so I shall still lose money. Well, they accepted

that offer and he carried on. This man is making fine footwear. He has to import a certain proportion of his materials from foreign countries, Europe and South America, through New York; and, of course, all his accounts are payable on bills of exchange in New York. He vsent to the Receiver General at Montreal to get gold and could not get it. He went to the bank, and took some bills issued by this government in the name of the crown and stamped payable in gold-one hundred dollar bills, five hundred dollar bills and one thousand dollar bills. He then said to the Receiver General, "Here is the promise of the crown of England and the government of Canada to pay in gold; will you give me gold for it?" What was the answer? "No, sir; we have orders from Ottawa not to give any gold." And so he had to pay an increased rate in New York of twenty per cent in order to keep his men alive. Is that speculation? I fail to see that, on behalf of Canada, an emergency exists for such measures, exists just now, and let me assure the Prime Minister that so far as Quebec is concerned, if nobody suffered from cold or hunger, it is not due to his administration-though I willingly acknowledge his sincerity in this connection- but it is due, among the farming classes, especially to Providence, and in our towns, to cur lay and religious organizations both Catholic and Protestant. Without these two factors, we would have had to register in Quebec the saddest disaster in our history.
I understand this measure to be a temporary one, and I trust that it will be the last of its kind introduced by the Prime Minister, if he wishes us to be more agreeable in our comments in the future. I wish to protest both on behalf of my constituency and myself against this radical way of administering the country, for I was unable to discover in the arguments of the leader of the government any urgent motive which could authorize him to make use of such radical methods, as those we are asked to approve to-day.
Mr. ELIE-O. BERTRAND (Prescott) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, I deem it my duty to protest against the resolution submitted to the house. There is certainly no doubt that the government is at present very much embarrassed to find means to relieve the unemployed and at the same time assist the farmers. But it is also true that there are other means to relieve them than by laying hands on the legislative powers of Parliament and creating a dictatorship when this house is in session.
At the risk of repeating what was stated by other speakers who preceded me in this debate, I shall narrate the political history of the Conservative party from the day they assumed power. First, without going back

Unemployment Continuance Act
too far in the past, I nevertheless wish to briefly state again the pledges given in the course of the last election, and remind the house that, at the 1930 election, the leader of the Conservative party travelled from one end of the country to the other, stating that the depression which was everywhere was due to the nine years of bad administration under the Liberal regime; he added that when given power he would find means to relieve the situation and bring back the country to its normal state. Addressing himself to the unemployed he pledged himself to find work for all those who wished to work and that their labours would be well remunerated; turning to the farmers, he told them that he would see to it that their products would bring in far better returns than during the last years of the Liberal regime.
The people believed to a certain extent these fine pledges because, already, the country was feeling the first pangs of the worldwide depression. The Liberal leader had made preparations to ward off this depression when it would reach our country, and through the medium of Hon. Mr. Dunning's budget had found it possible to reach the various markets of the Empire, establish better trade relations so as to later spread our trade to all markets of the world. In order to attain this end the Liberal government thought it good policy to make concessions so as to receive some from other countries.
The Conservative party, having assumed power, considered that this policy was absolutely wrong and wishing to follow up their cry of "Canada First," made a complete change. It also had made very fabulous pledges in connection with the tariff and had assured the people that with a high tariff, industries would flourish, and, the latter being prosperous the working classes would have work and would be in a position to purchase farm products, the result would be that all classes of the community would enjoy a prosperity unknown until then. These pledges were so alluring that people believed in them.
The unemployment situation having become worse, notwithstanding all the pledges given to the unemployed throughout Canada, the leader of the Conservative party called a special session for September, 1930. This short session was intended to relieve the depression as promised. The people were under the impression that pursuant to the pledges made, day labour would be given to all those who wanted to work and thus increasing the purchasing power, the farmer would easily sell his products. However, the remedy was not as effective as one could have expected. The

special session having been called, parliament met and the Conservative party introduced a measure in which they requested $20,000,000 for unemployment relief. Although this session was called specifically to discuss unemployment, a bill dealing with extraordinary changes in the tariff was also introduced; almost every item of the tariff schedule was altered; the greatest protection was given to people in industries and manufacturers. The time had arrived when these people expected to see manna fall from heaven. Often in the past they had asked for higher tariff, but never had they obtained it and never had they expected to obtain as much as they were given at that special session.
Did this protection give the good results which were anticipated? For a while it may have stimulated business, but in the wake of the world-wide depression they soon realized that it became more and more difficult to sell their products abroad. I shall not insist on the meagre results obtained at the Imperial Economic Conference, in London, by the Prime Minister and his lieutenants. This failure was not of a nature to increase our trade with the other countries of the empire. Our purchasing power having decreased, the business people and manufacturers found themselves also in a critical position and were unable to find a market for their products.
Let us examine how these measures were adopted. They were enacted within a few days after the Conservative leader, who had begun to reveal himself under his true light, as we know him to-day, had stated: You must necessarily adopt these measures; they must be enacted within a few days, because otherwise I shall not attend the Imperial Economic Conference. The following suggestion was made by the leader of the opposition: Allow some of your leading lieutenants to remain in Canada, we shall carry on with the session and you will be free to attend the Imperial conference. I wish to be present here myself, retorted the Prime Minister, and these measures must appear in the Statutes of the Dominion of Canada previous to my departure. Already the leader of the Conservative party was showing signs of his predilection for a dictatorship. He was not yet known under his true light, however, signs were not wanting that, little by little, he would lay hands on all the privileges and prerogatives of the Canadian parliament.
In order to convince the house and Canada that this government had not made a deep study of the needs of the country, it is only necessary to recall that, after having

had $20,000,000 voted to relieve the unemployed, by the end of the -fiscal year only $4,400,000 had been expended, namely, from September to the end of March. There still remained more than $15,000,000 which has not been utilized. This proves that the government was not in touch with the situation and was ignorant of the needs of the unemployed. The fiscal year having expired, instead of having other amounts voted, as it was done later on they continued to spend what remained of the $20,000,000, and according to the statement made by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), a sum of over $15,000,000 was thus distributed.
I again state that from then on we could foresee what the Conservative leader's attitude would be; at the time, the Prime Minister not wishing that his own followers should discover that their leader was really a dictator making them yield little by little to his will and gradually inuring them to his methods, began by having them adopt the $20,000,000 measure so as to, later, obtain their assent in having the house enact all the bills that he might wish to introduce.
At the 1931 session, after sitting in camera over public affairs, he came before parliament and instead of conforming himself to custom and usage by asking that a fixed amount be voted either in the budget or through special legislation, for a specific end, as he had done, in 1930, with the idea of having people believe that he intended to carry out his electoral pledges and thus amazed them by amounts as fabulous as his pledges, he refuses to specify an amount. We shall he says, take all the necessary money to solve the problems with which we shall have to deal, not only do we ask for all the funds necessary, but we still want more. We want to have this money voted by a special act which will authorize us to deal, by order in council, with all the business we see fit, and which will empower us to amend the acts adopted by parliament and that are the exclusive prerogative of the latter. We wish to have the full control over public affairs for peace, order and good government throughout the dominion.
The people therefore thought that, that Conservative party had not only $20,000,000 at its disposal but an unlimited amount which would help in bringing back prosperity. First, $20,000,000 were asked at the special session of 1930, and later a blank cheque was requested at the 1931 session; yet after all this, they inform us that no remedy can be found to relieve the depression. People are wondering what they will request at the next session. This is the natural consequence of the dictatorship inflicted on the house.
We protest, sir, against this resolution which reads as follows:
That the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into rommittee of the whole on the following resolution:
Certain newspapers of this country contend that, this resolution is absolutely harmless and that it should not lend itself to any criticism on the part of the opposition. However, when one scrutinizes it more closely, when one is made aware of what happened under the dictatorship which began at the 1931 session, and which has become more exacting this session, we are entitled to wonder what will be the result.
According to the statement made the other day by the hen. Minister of Labour, in the house, the government authorized, by order in council, in the course of the year 1931, the expenditure of an amount totalling $32,800,000 so as to meet the obligations contracted to relieve the unemployed, and out of this amount of $32,800,000, 7,415,973 days of work were provided for 334,301 persons, or 22f days to each person. Is it possible to imagine such a wretched result under such a dictatorship: only 22 days of work for each person employed by virtue of the unemployment relief act, adopted in 1931.	$32,800,000 seems a very
large amount to a labourer whose wages are $2 or $3 per day; he has no idea what it represents. The labourer is told that the government spent $32,800,000 which furnished 7,415,973 days of work to Canadians from March, 1931, to February, 1932; this seems a great achievement, however if the hon. Minister of Labour had been in earnest, he would have added that this amount only represented 22f days of work for each person, he would have further stated that the Dominion government in making the outlay of $32,800,000 had obliged the provinces to subscribe an equal amount, if not a larger one, and that the municipalities had been forced to contribute an amount equal to that of both governments, provincial and federal. Notwithstanding all these outlays the depression has further spread since; according to statistics compiled by the "Child and Family Welfare Journal," the number of unemployed in Canada actually varies between
400,000	and 450,000.
Weighing these facts and noting how agriculture is languishing everywhere, one easily realizes that agriculture did not receive the necessary aid. It has been asserted that in the province of Saskatchewan there has been no crop, this explains why the farmers of that province are in great difficulty. Such a situation however should not exist where crops

have not failed, yet the facts are there to prove, that even the farmers of Ontario are almost bankrupt. I shall have an opportunity of referring again to Ontario when the agriculture estimates are before the house or when the budget is brought down. I shall simply state to-day that the farmers are unable to meet their obligations because they cannot even sell their products at cost price. Owing to this fact, their purchasing power has greatly dwindled and they find themselves in a difficult situation. Their condition is so critical that the Ontario government has recently adopted a measure to prevent the sale, by creditors, of farmers' lands which are mortgaged. They can be forced to pay the interest and taxes, but not the capital. Otherwise the situation would become intolerable, and farmers in most cases would be despoiled of their possessions. Considering the difficult situation in which our people find themselves at present notwithstanding the $20,000,000 voted last session, and the unlimited amount requested at the 1931 session, or the pledges made by the leader of the Conservative party to relieve unemployment and assist agriculture as he stated at Moncton, New Brunswick on July 10, 1930:
The Conservative party is going to find work for all who are willing to work or perish in the attempt.
Could we not request the Prime Minister to implement his pledge. Instead of introducing an arbitrary measure, he should admit that he failed in his task and that he is ready to appeal to the people to find out whether they endorse his conduct when he requests this Parliament to despoil itself of all its prerogatives, so as to allow him to adopt or amend any act according to his whims, or again, to vote him unlimited amounts without previously submitting estimates or stating how they will be spent. I think it would be most interesting to make an appeal to the people in this connection.
The leader of the Conservative party also stated at Moncton:
Mr. King promises to study the unemployment problem; I pledge myself to put an end to unemployment. Which plan do you like best.
I put it to the house and the country whether it would not have been wiser to first study the unemployment problem, follow the suggestions made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and then deal with this problem in the right way rather than use half measures.
It would be quite to the purpose to apply to-day, to the right hon. Prime Minister the

words he used when speaking at Vancouver, on June 18, 1930, as published in the Montreal Gazette, the following day:
However blind he may be to your future, and deaf to your present needs, surely he cannot stop his ears with smug compliance and self-esteem to the cry that carries across the nation-the cry of destitute and hungry, the cry of mothers and fathers and little children who call to us as Christians and as Canadians to heal their pain.
That is the kind of appeal which the Prime Minister made at the last election, what has he to say, to-day? That this crisis is worldwide and difficult to deal with. What does he want to-day? He wishes to extend the life of this Act by which he arrogates to himself all authority and, together with the cabinet in council, he wishes to have a free hand, even when Parliament is sitting. We must, sir, as representatives of the people strongly protest against the principle of his Act. We however, find no fault with the following words included in the resolution:
That the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole on the following resolution:
But we are opposed to the following principle laid down by this resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a bill to amend chapter 58 of the statutes of Canada, 1931, striking out the word "March" in section 8, and substituting the word "May" therefor.
This may seem of no consequence to those who are not acquainted with the provisions of chapter 58 of the Statutes of Canada, 1931. They are unaware that this means the placing at the disposal of the government of unlimited amounts; they are ignorant of the fact that this Act empowers them to pass whatever orders in council they please, either to amend our laws or favour any industry without the consent of Parliament or without the representatives of the people having anything to say in the matter. It simply amounts to a dictatorship, especially when Parliament is in session. When Parliament is not sitting, perhaps there can be some excuse for assuming such powers, as unforeseen cases may arise necessitating special measures, however, when Parliament is in session, it is perfectly ridiculous to request such powers. These methods remind us of the time when we were governed by the Family Compact, and when the Canadian people had not the right to elect their representatives who were appointed by the State. To-day, the representatives of the

people are not chosen by the State, but measures are enacted by the government without the consent of Parliament.
What is the difference between the policy of this government, led by the present Prime Minister, and that of the Family Compact which ruled when our forebears demanded liberty, claimed their rights and wished to establish in this country the justice and fair play which characterizes British legislation or when they insisted to be given in this country a constitution which would enable the people to have a voice in all matters through their representatives?
I do not wish to stir up any feelings over this question, on the contrary, I simply wish to point out our views on the principle involved. We wish, without playing politics, to strongly protest in the House and throughout the country against the principle set forth by the Family Compact, and thus follow in the footsteps of the champions of the early days of the colony. W'e are fortunate to have had as an example, Papineau in Quebec and Mackenzie in Ontario, to champion the rights of our people.
The government, sir, wishes to have our cooperation to enact this measure. We are willing to cooperate in every way possible. However, as stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), what kind of a cooperation does the government expect? They ask us to entrust everything to them, to vote an unlimited amount; and later on they will inform us, through the Prime Minister, what was decided by order in council. What further cooperation do they ask? To afford them the means, still through orders in council, to upset our statutes as they please, whether it is a question of insurance, gold export, the Bank Act or other important laws upon which depend the whole economic situation and the welfare of our people. Like our forebears we must strongly oppose this dictatorship and protect our people in order that they may enjoy their liberty and that our Parliament may preserve intact its prerogatives.
